lead: A pointer that swings across a scale is pushed by a magnetic force on a current-carrying part. In a moving-coil meter that part is a coil inside a permanent magnet, and the swing is proportional to current. In a moving-iron meter that part is a piece of soft iron pulled into a coil, and the swing is proportional to current squared. The first suits DC and laboratory work. The second also works on AC and sits on cheap panel boards. Both still exist behind the digital display.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 current, resistance and Ohm's law; Unit 2 RMS value and phasors for the AC behaviour of these meters.

sections.h3: The three torques, and the moving-coil meter

blocks.text: An indicating instrument needs three torques. The deflecting torque moves the pointer away from zero. The controlling torque pulls it back, so the pointer stops where the two balance. The damping torque acts only while the pointer is moving, so it settles quickly instead of swinging.

In a permanent-magnet moving-coil (PMMC) meter a light coil of N turns and area A m² sits in the gap of a permanent magnet. A soft iron cylinder fills the gap, so the flux density B (tesla) is radial and always cuts the coil sides at right angles. A current I (ampere) through the coil gives the deflecting torque below.
T = N B I A    and    T = k θ    so    θ = (N B A / k) I
blocks.where: T is deflecting torque in N m; N is the number of turns; B is flux density in T; I is coil current in A; A is coil area in m²; k is the spring constant in N m per radian; θ is deflection in radians.

blocks.text: A hairspring gives a controlling torque proportional to the angle and also carries current into the coil. At balance the two torques are equal, so deflection is proportional to current and the scale is uniform. An aluminium former on the coil produces eddy currents as it moves; that is the damping. Jewelled bearings keep friction low, so a movement of 50 μA full scale is practical. Some syllabi call this the D'Arsonval movement.

A moving-iron meter has a stationary coil and a small piece of soft iron that moves. In the attraction type the iron disc is pulled into the coil, and the pointer turns with it. In the repulsion type two iron vanes sit inside the coil, one fixed and one on the spindle. The coil magnetises both vanes in the same direction, so they repel and the moving vane swings.

blocks.where: T is deflecting torque in N m; I is coil current in A; L is the inductance of the coil in H, which changes as the iron vane moves; dL/dθ is the rate of change of inductance with deflection θ in radians. Torque therefore goes as I².

blocks.text: The square law has two consequences. First, reversing the current leaves the torque in the same direction, so the meter works on AC. Second, on AC the average torque follows the mean square of the current, so the meter reads the RMS value directly and gives the same reading on AC and DC for the same heating effect.

The cost is the scale: deflection goes as I², so divisions are cramped near zero and wide near full scale. Iron adds hysteresis and eddy-current errors, the reading drifts with frequency, and stray fields disturb it. Against that, the meter is cheap, robust, has no magnet to weaken, and can be built for large currents.

sections.h3: Range extension, and a moving-coil meter on AC

blocks.text: A PMMC movement has a small full-scale current I_m, often 50 μA to 1 mA, and its own resistance R_m. To read a larger current, connect a low resistance R_sh in parallel. This is the shunt, and most of the current bypasses the coil.

blocks.where: I is the current to be measured in A; I_m is the full-scale current of the movement in A; R_m is the movement resistance in Ω; R_sh is the shunt resistance in Ω.
V is the voltage to be measured in V; I_m is the full-scale current in A; R_m is the movement resistance in Ω; R_se is the series multiplier resistance in Ω.

blocks.text: The multiplier R_se is connected in series, so the full-scale current flows when the rated voltage is applied. On AC the current reverses every half cycle, the torque reverses, and the pointer stays at zero. A bridge rectifier in front of the coil fixes the direction, and the meter then reads the average of the rectified current. For a sine wave, average = 0.637 I_peak and RMS = 0.707 I_peak; their ratio, the form factor 1.11, is built into the scale. That reading is correct only for a sine wave. A moving-iron meter needs no rectifier and reads RMS of any waveform.

PMMC movements sit in laboratory ammeters and voltmeters, analog multimeters and galvanometers. Moving-iron meters appear on switchboard panel meters and cheap clamp meters, where ruggedness matters more than accuracy.

figure.caption: Deflection as a fraction of full scale for two 5 A ammeters. The moving-coil line is straight; the moving-iron curve rises as the square of current, so it is still only 16% of full scale at 2 A.

spec.aria: A straight line shows moving-coil deflection rising linearly with current; a curve shows moving-iron deflection rising as current squared, using a 5 A full scale.

examples.question: Two ammeters have the same full-scale current of 5 A. One is a moving-coil meter with θ ∝ I; the other is a moving-iron meter with θ ∝ I². (a) Find the deflection as a fraction of full scale at 2 A for each. (b) Find the current at which the moving-iron meter reaches half scale.
steps: Moving coil: fraction of full scale = θ/θ_FS = I/I_FS = 2 A / 5 A = 0.4, that is 40% of full scale.
Moving iron: fraction = (I/I_FS)² = (2/5)² = 0.4² = 0.16, that is 16% of full scale.
Half scale on the moving-iron meter: (I/5)² = 0.5, so I/5 = √0.5 = 0.7071.
examples.answer: At 2 A the moving-coil meter shows 0.4 of full scale (40%) and the moving-iron meter 0.16 (16%); the moving-iron meter reaches half scale only at 3.54 A.
examples.check:
import math
I = 2.0
I_fs = 5.0
mc = I / I_fs
mi = (I / I_fs) ** 2
i_half = I_fs * math.sqrt(0.5)
print(round(mc, 4))
print(round(mi, 4))
print(round(i_half, 2))

traps: Writing θ ∝ 2I for a moving-iron meter. The torque goes as current squared, not twice the current: at 2 A on a 5 A meter the fraction is (2/5)² = 0.16, not 0.4.

Expecting a PMMC meter to read AC directly. Without a rectifier the torque reverses every half cycle and the pointer stays at zero; with a rectifier it reads 1.11 × average, which equals RMS only for a sine wave.

Swapping shunt and multiplier. The shunt goes in parallel with the movement (ammeter) and is small; the multiplier goes in series (voltmeter) and is large. The wrong one gives a wrong reading or a burnt coil.
Assuming a moving-iron meter reads average on AC. It responds to I², so it reads RMS.
Using only the full-scale current or only the coil resistance in a range formula. Both I_m and R_m are needed: R_sh = I_m R_m/(I − I_m) and R_se = V/I_m − R_m.

quiz.q: State what the deflection of a moving-coil meter is proportional to, and what the deflection of a moving-iron meter is proportional to.
quiz.a: Moving coil: θ ∝ I. Moving iron: θ ∝ I².

quiz.q: Name the three torques needed in an indicating instrument, and state what provides damping in a PMMC meter.
quiz.a: Deflecting torque, controlling torque and damping torque. A light aluminium former on the coil gives eddy-current damping.

quiz.q: Why does a PMMC meter read zero on a 50 Hz AC supply with no rectifier?
quiz.a: The current reverses each half cycle, so the deflecting torque reverses. The coil cannot follow at 50 Hz, the average torque is zero, and the pointer rests at zero.

quiz.q: Why is the moving-iron scale cramped near zero?
quiz.a: Deflection depends on I², so equal steps of current give unequal steps of angle; the divisions are narrow at low current and wide near full scale, which makes low readings hard to read.

quiz.q: A PMMC movement has full-scale current 1 mA and resistance 100 Ω. Find the shunt needed to read 10 mA full scale.
The same movement (1 mA, 100 Ω) must read 10 V full scale. Find the series multiplier.
A moving-iron meter and a rectifier-type moving-coil meter are both calibrated on a sine wave and read 230 V. What does each read on a square wave of the same RMS value?
quiz.a: The moving-iron meter still reads 230 V because it responds to mean square, which is true RMS. The rectified moving-coil meter reads 1.11 × average; for a square wave average equals RMS, so it reads about 1.11 × 230 = 255 V, roughly 11% high.

quiz.q: Why does reversing the current not reverse the reading of a moving-iron meter, while it drives a PMMC pointer backwards?
quiz.a: Moving-iron torque depends on I², which stays positive when I reverses, so direction does not matter. PMMC torque depends on the sign of I, so a reversed current reverses the torque and pushes the pointer off scale.

beyond: Not for the exam. Analog movements survive where a cheap, always-on indication matters: switchboard panel meters, automotive ammeters and analog multimeters. Modern designs sense current with a shunt plus an ADC, or with a Hall-effect sensor, and compute the value digitally. Every commercial instrument carries an accuracy class, and calibration laboratories check it against a standard. True-RMS meters do the squaring and averaging electronically, which is exactly what the moving-iron vane did with mechanics. Search next for accuracy class of indicating instruments, true-RMS measurement, and shunt sizing.
